Baseline PCA measures the variance in

the largest and most active subnetwork
bPCA corrects for redundancy and noise
bPCA compares the test data against two baselines:
Noise baseline: the variance due to the measurement process alone
Redundancy baseline: the system measured with the constraint of interest removed
bPCA finds the family of projections
Eigenvalues are test variance above the noise floor, in units of the redundancy baseline (negative
eigenvalues are dropped: +); PCA, cPCA and ρPCA are thus limiting cases.
Earlier contrastive methods can be thought of as comparing the test data with a single baseline [3, 4]:
bPCA subtracts noise covariance, whitens corrected redundancy, then orthogonalizes the test data:
Ratio methods such as ρPCA divide two covariances, amplifying directions dominated by noise
Subtractive methods such as cPCA subtract two covariances, but require hyperparameter tuning
We decoded the direction of drifting gratings (0°, 45°, 90° or 135°, 10% contrast; 75 trials
each) from Neuropixels recordings of mouse visual cortex (Allen Visual Coding, Functional
Connectivity set [5]; 23 sessions; 18 male, 5 female mice), pooling all visual cortical units.
Test data: trial-mean firing rates during gratings
Redundancy baseline: spontaneous activity, partitioned into trial-length windows
Noise baseline: counting noise of firing rates, from spontaneous spikes (below)
(d) Noise dominates fast fluctuations, so short windows can be used to estimate noise covariance.
(e) We measure noise covariance from spontaneous spikes in 10 ms bins, scaled up to a trial-mean
rate, which has a median of 23% of units' trial-mean variance.
Above: (f) Trial-mean responses of an example session (537
units) on its two leading PCA components; colors mark grating
direction and crosses the class means.
(g) The same session on its two leading bPCA components.
(h) Error in decoding direction from the top k components
times; mean ± SD across 23 sessions; dashed line: chance).
With spontaneous activity as the redundancy baseline, bPCA concentrates stimulus
information into its leading components, cutting the mean two-component error by 23°.
Temporal autocorrelation pervades neural and behavioral time series, and PCA of
autocorrelated signals returns smooth, sinusoid-like components (phantom oscillations)
[6]. We simulated 200 signals that share a weak, chaotic latent, on top of independent 1/f
background activity and a shared instrument artifact.
Redundancy baseline: phase-randomized (IAAFT) surrogates [7], which preserve
autocorrelation but scramble the shared latent
Noise baseline: a calibration recording of the instrument only
(a) The leading PCA component is a slow phantom oscillation (ρ = 0.06 with the latent), whereas the
leading bPCA component recovers the latent (ρ = 0.88). Given the same redundancy baseline, cPCA
(ρ = 0.07) and ρPCA (ρ = 0.05) also fail (medians over 100 simulations).
(b) Held-out eigenvalues (medians across 100 simulations): the two leading PCA eigenvalues are
nearly equal, as for phantom oscillations, whereas the bPCA eigenvalues fall to the baseline level of
